essential: Tommy enters the filthy house and climbs the stairs. He reasons that 'Mr. Brown' is a password, and that entering the meeting room risks a further password or proof of identity.
He hides in the curtained recess opposite the meeting-room door, which also overlooks the stairs. Keep its position and the rents in the curtain that let him watch.

He watches the arrivals. A brutish criminal answers 'Fourteen' to the bearded, precise-voiced German chairing the table ('Your number, comrade?' / 'Correct'), and Tommy is glad he did not walk in. Then come an Irish Sinn Feiner, a shabby city-clerk type, a working man whose face is vaguely familiar, and an exquisitely dressed, commanding man whose face is also familiar but unnamed.
Tommy reflects on how far-reaching and strange this chain of links under Mr. Brown is.

The last arrival is a small, pale man with a hissing voice and Slavonic cheekbones. His eyes seem to burn through the curtain and make Tommy shiver; he likens him to a venomous snake. He is received with deference as 'Number One'. Do NOT name him or hint at his public identity.
Number One asks for Mr. Brown. The German says Brown cannot attend in person, leaving the sentence oddly unfinished. Number One suggests Brown may be among them, and the men eye each other in fear.

The door is shut. Tommy removes his shoes, fails to open the locked door, carefully restores the handle, then gets into the adjoining bedroom. He draws the rusty bolt of the communicating door and can hear through a portière but not see.

Overheard business, kept in summary: Irish money and ammunition, with money routed via Irish Americans and 'Mr. Potter' (an American voice notes waning sympathy); a loan to an English newspaper with Moscow denial; union reports (miners satisfactory, hold back railways).
The date is the 29th, set by the Labour leaders, who must believe it their own show. Include Number One's 'honest men' remarks.
Clymes 'must go'; Number Fourteen will see to it, wearing gloves with a housebreaker's prints, and he relishes blood in the streets.

The German admits the honest Labour leaders may not strike, because public opinion favours the Government. A certain document would assure success, but they do not have it. Perhaps only 'a girl' knows where it is; 'This case is different'. As the German begins to say where she is, Tommy is struck down from behind. The attacker is unseen.

title: THE ADVENTURES OF TOMMY
voice_profile: Brisk, comic third-person narration in close focus on one young adventurer at a time. It works through quick dialogue tags ('snarled', 'sweetly', 'moralized'), slangy period banter ('old bean', 'keep her end up', 'a dirty trick!'), and wry narrative asides that undercut the heroics: Tuppence admiring her own ingenuity, or Tommy reasoning 'in his usual slow and steady way'. Suspense comes from short paragraphs, dashes, trailing ellipses and abrupt chapter-end cliffhangers. Characters are often 'telling the truth' in ways others misread. Menace is conveyed through physical tells such as shifty eyes, purpling faces and a sibilant voice, and through ironic political epigram.
book_context: A 1920s thriller built on the joint venture of Tommy and Tuppence. Chapters alternate between their separate adventures and end on cliffhangers. Recurring mechanisms include accidental truth-telling that works as a bluff; names dropped casually that become clues ('Jane Finn', 'Rita', the clerk 'Brown'); and the faceless 'Mr. Brown', always suspected to be an unnoticed person present in the room. The approaching date of the 29th drives the plot. Chapter II plants the clues that Carter and Tuppence later decode in IV and VI. Chapter VIII plants the date, the conspirators' faces, Jane's mysterious incapacity and the recess hiding-place, all of which pay off in XVI, XVII and the climax in XXVI–XXVII. Abridgment must keep these plants without explaining them early.
